title: On the existence of consistent adversarial attacks in high-dimensional linear classification
claim: Adversarial perturbations differ by whether they change only the model's prediction or also the true label.
layout: Single 2-D scatter panel, two callout boxes at bottom, arrows pointing up
description: A single 2-D toy sketch on a cream rounded panel titled 'Consistent vs. Inconsistent Adversarial Perturbations'. Blue dots (Class B) sit in the upper half and red dots (Class A) in the lower half. A solid black line is labeled the learnt model boundary. A dashed line crossing it is labeled the ground truth boundary. Two points are perturbed with arrows. X moves left to X', which stays blue and so on the correct side of the ground-truth boundary but crosses the model boundary. Y moves down to Y', which crosses both boundaries and turns red. Two rounded callout boxes at the bottom, with arrows pointing to X' and Y', label them as a consistent adversarial example (changes the prediction but preserves the true class) and an inconsistent one (changes both the prediction and the ground-truth class). The eye goes first to the coloured dots and arrows.
caption: Illustration of the difference between consistent Adversarial Perturbation and inconsistent Adversarial Perturbation.
abstract: What fundamentally distinguishes an adversarial attack from a misclassification due to limited model expressivity or finite data? In this work, we investigate this question in the setting of high-dimensional binary classification, where statistical effects due to limited data availability play a central role. We introduce a new error metric that precisely capture this distinction, quantifying model vulnerability to consistent adversarial attacks -- perturbations that preserve the ground-truth labels. Our main technical contribution is an exact and rigorous asymptotic characterization of these metrics in both well-specified models and latent space models, revealing different vulnerability patterns compared to standard robust error measures. The theoretical results demonstrate that as models become more overparameterized, their vulnerability to label-preserving perturbations grows, offering theoretical insight into the mechanisms underlying model sensitivity to adversarial attacks.
